title: What makes you happy?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Since its origins in a Leipzig laboratory 130 years ago, psychology has had little to say about goodness and contentment. Mostly psychologists have concerned themselves with weakness and misery. There are libraries full of theories about why we get sad, worried, and angry. It hasn't been respectable science to study what happens when lives go well. Positive experiences, such as joy, kindness, altruism and heroism have mainly been ignored.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A few pioneers in experimental psychology have bucked the trend. Professor Alice Isen of Cornell University and colleagues have shown how positive emotions make people think faster and more creatively, Demonstrating how easy it is to give people an intellectual boost, Isen divided doctors making a tricky diagnosis into three groups: one received candy, one read humanistic statements about medicine, one was a control group. The doctors who had candy displayed the most creative thinking and worked more efficiently.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Inspired by Isen and others, Martin Seligman, an American professor psychology and author of 'Authentic Happiness', has become a leading figure in the field of positive psychology. He has raised millions of dollars of research money and funded 50 research groups involving 150 scientists from a range of countries, Their research has discovered six core virtues recognised in all cultures: wisdom, courage, humanity, justice, temperance and transcendence. These have been subdivided into 24 strengths, including humour and honesty.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: But some scientists are demanding answers to big questions. What is the point of defining levels of happiness and classifying the virtues? Aren't these concepts vague and impossible to pin down? Can you justify spending funds to research positive states when we have an increasing number of people suffering from depression? Seligman knows his work can be belittled alongside trite notions such as 'The power of positive thinking', His plan to stop the new science floating 'on the waves of self-improvement fashions' is to make sure it is anchored to positive philosophy above, and to positive biology below. And this takes us back to our evolutionary past.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Homo sapiens evolved during the Pleistocene era (1.8m to 10,000 years ago), a time of hardship and turmoil. Survival in a time of adversity forged our brains into a persistent mould. Professor Seligman says, 'We evolved during a time of ice, flood and famine and our brain is best described as catastrophic. The way the brain works is looking for what's wrong. The Problem is, that worked in the Pleistocene era. It favoured you, but it doesn't work in the modern world.'

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Although most people rate themselves as happy, there is a wealth of evidence to show that negative thinking is deeply ingrained in the human psyche. Of the six universal emotions, four — anger, fear, disgust and sadness — are negative and only one, joy, is positive. (The sixth , surprise, is neutral.) According to the psychologist Daniel Nettle, the negative emotions each tell us 'something bad has happened' and prompt a different course of action. Fear tells us to run away, while anger prompts us to deter aggressors. But joy, according to Nettle, simply tells us 'something good has happened, don't change anything.'.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What is it about the structure of the brain that underlies our bias towards negative thinking? And is there a biology of joy? At Iowa University, neuroscientists studied what happens when people are shown pleasant and unpleasant pictures. When subjects saw landscapes or dolphins playing, part of the frontal lobe of the brain became active. But when they were shown unpleasant images — a bird covered in oil, for example — there was activity in more primitive parts of the brain. The ability to feel negative emotions derives from an ancient danger-recognition system formed early in the brain's evolution. The pre-frontal cortex, which registers happiness, is the part used for higher thinking, an area that evolved later in human history.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Professor Richard Davidson at the University of Wisconsin has scanned brains in different emotional states. Observing toddlers at play, he picked some who were exuberant and uninhibited, behaviour associated with higher levels of positive emotion and others who were quiet and shy. Tested later, the inhibited toddlers showed greater activity on the brain's right side; activation of the lively toddlers' brains was on the left. Happiness and sadness are lopsided.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: Modern humans, stuck with an ancient brain, are like rats on a wheel. We can't stop running because we're always looking over our shoulders and comparing our achievements with our neighbours'. This is called the 'hedonic treadmill' by happiness scholars. We dwell on what went badly, not what went well When life runs smoothly, we're on autopilot. It causes us to adapt rapidly and inevitably to good things by taking them for granted. The more possessions and accomplishments we have, the more we need. to boost our level of happiness. By a trick of nature our brains are designed to crave but never really achieve lasting happiness.
